column4: The source section's root خ ش ع and its gloss of a gaze lowered to earth recur in خُشَّعًا أَبْصَارُهُمْ: people emerge from graves with humbled eyes, the same bodily scene the section draws from.
The section names خ ش ع for eyes cast down; here أَبْصَارُهَا خَاشِعَةٌ gives that posture at the Day of Resurrection, after the preceding verse's trembling faces.
The section directly cites this image: wrongdoers shown to the fire look from a hidden corner of the eye, يَنظُرُونَ مِن طَرْفٍ خَفِيٍّ. It makes the gaze itself a sign of humiliation.
The section's خ ش ع eye posture appears as خَاشِعَةً أَبْصَارُهُمْ, with disgrace overtaking those who cannot raise their gaze.
The source section's root خ ش ع is applied directly to eyes here: خَاشِعَةً أَبْصَارُهُمْ, as disgrace overtakes those facing judgment.
The section's hidden eye-corner glance is reversed by God's knowledge of خَائِنَةَ الْأَعْيُنِ: a stealthy look is hidden from people but exposed to divine sight.
The source section quotes the dictionary example ينظرون إليك وهم لا يبصرون; this ayah says idols seem to look at the observer but do not see, directly distinguishing looking from perceiving.
The source section contrasts reflective النظر with merely looking; this verse says some look at the Prophet but remain blind, so sight alone does not become understanding.
The section asks for a seeing that considers creation; here people have eyes لا يُبْصِرُونَ بِهَا and hearts that do not understand, a direct boundary between eyes and perception.
The section contrasts today's available gaze with the coming reckoning; here the veil is removed and sight becomes sharp, revealing what a person had failed to see.
After 53:17 defines the gaze as neither diverted nor excessive, this verse says it saw the greatest signs of its Lord; the cited ayah gives the object of that disciplined sight.
The source section explicitly names this as the farthest destination of النظر: faces on that Day look toward their Lord, إِلَىٰ رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ.
The section cites this raised, free gaze: people reclining on couches look around, عَلَى الْأَرَائِكِ يَنظُرُونَ, a paradise counterpart to eyes cast down.
The source section explicitly notes that the spring noun عَيْن also means eye; here one spring splits into twelve, making the spring-as-eye word audible in a scene of gushing water.
This repeated account calls the water sources عَيْنًا and says twelve gush forth; it repeats the source section's eye-and-spring double sense in a concrete flow scene.
The source section names عَيْن as both eye and spring; here the setting sun appears to go down into a muddy spring, joining the eye's visible horizon to the water-source word.
The source section's water definition for the root ع ي ن is water apparent to eyes; this verse's مَعِين is a spring beside a settled height, a clear counterpart to that visible-water sense.

The source section's root ع ي ن links eye and spring; here سليمان is given an عَيْنَ الْقِطْرِ, a spring/source of molten copper, extending the image from flowing water to a visible issuing substance.
The source section's عين double sense appears in two running springs, عَيْنَانِ تَجْرِيَانِ, a direct image of visible flowing water.
This verse repeats the root ع ي ن for two springs, now described as gushing; it gives a second, more forceful form of the spring flow named by the section.
The section explains the spring-related sense of the root as water apparent to eyes; this verse asks who could bring back مَاءٍ مَعِينٍ, visibly available flowing water.
The source section hears eye in the noun عَيْن; this verse presents a spring from which God's servants drink and which they cause to flow abundantly.
The source section quotes this same question: look at the sky above and how it was built, أَفَلَمْ يَنظُرُوا إِلَى السَّمَاءِ فَوْقَهُمْ كَيْفَ بَنَيْنَاهَا, an exact parallel to looking at creation.
After 50:6 directs the gaze to the sky, this verse supplies the earth below: it was spread out, anchored with mountains, and made to grow varied plants.
Continuing 50:7's visible earth, this verse shows rain from above producing gardens, grain, and tall palms, making the earth's provision observable.
The section's free النظر is made literal in ارْجِعِ الْبَصَرَ: people are told to inspect the layered skies and see whether they contain a flaw.
After 67:3 orders another look at the sky, this verse says to repeat the gaze; it returns exhausted, giving the act of looking its limit and result.
This verse directly commands, انظُرُوا مَاذَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ, to look at what is in the heavens and earth, the same open field of sight as 88:17, 88:18, 88:19, and 88:20.

The source section quotes this question about looking into the dominion of the heavens and earth; its close asks what report people will believe afterward, connecting observation with the surah's opening hadith.
The section quotes the command to travel the earth and see how creation began; this verse explicitly joins that looking to God's later creation, making observation evidence for resurrection.
The section quotes this command to look at God's mercy in reviving earth after its death; the visible return of life makes the gaze a sign of the later return.
This verse asks the reader to see varied fruits, then describes colored mountain bands; it brings the earth and raised mountains of the section into one observed scene.

Following the sight of fruits and mountains in 35:27, this verse includes people, animals, and cattle in the variety of creation and says those who know fear God; the camel in the section belongs to this living field.
The verse joins skies without visible supports, mountains set in the earth, and creatures spread across it, matching several directions of the section's creation-gaze.
This ayah's observed order includes heavens, earth, sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees, animals, and people; it gathers the same sky, mountain, earth, and creature field as the section.
The verse asks whether creating people or the sky was harder, opening a scene in which the raised sky, spread earth, mountains, and pasture are evidence of creation's power.
Continuing the creation question of 79:27, this verse says God raised and proportioned the sky, directly matching the section's upward gaze.
After the sky in 79:28 and 79:29, this verse says the earth was spread out, matching the section's downward gaze to the earth.
The continuation sets mountains firmly in place, matching the section's separate upward look at how mountains were raised.
The command فَلْيَنظُرِ الْإِنسَانُ مِمَّ خُلِقَ asks people to look at their own creation, closely paralleling the section's question about how the camel was created.
The section asks readers to inspect created beings; this verse commands people to look at fruit as it grows and ripens, أُنظُرُوا إِلَىٰ ثَمَرِهِ إِذَا أَثْمَرَ, a deliberate gaze at provision.
This verse directly commands, فَلْيَنظُرِ الْإِنسَانُ إِلَىٰ طَعَامِهِ, to inspect food, opening a close view of the earth's provision alongside the section's creation-gaze.
This verse says there are signs in the earth for those certain; it directly invites the earthward attention of the section's gaze.
After signs in the earth, this verse asks whether people see signs in themselves, extending the section's inspection of created beings inward.
The section cites the root خ ش ع for humbled eyes and a view of earth; here one sees the earth خَاشِعَةً before rain revives it, joining that root to the earth-and-revival scene.
This verse asks whether those who see the sky and earth's creation recognize God's ability to recreate people; it links the section's visible creation to return after death.
The verse asks whether the creator of heavens and earth can give life to the dead, directly joining the section's creation-gaze to its Day of Return.
The verse describes the earth as a bed, paths through it, and water from the sky producing varied plants; it gives concrete counterparts to the section's looks down and up.
The source section's lowered gaze is forced by the coming Day; here يَغُضُّوا مِنْ أَبْصَارِهِمْ commands men to lower their eyes now, making deliberate restraint a present counterpart.
The same root-and-eye detail appears in يَغْضُضْنَ مِنْ أَبْصَارِهِنَّ: women are told to lower their gaze by choice, a present boundary beside the section's humbled gaze in judgment.
The section's downcast gaze meets its reversal in تَشْخَصُ فِيهِ الْأَبْصَارُ: on the promised Day eyes stare in terror rather than falling toward earth.
The section shows eyes lowered on the Day; here the disbelievers' eyes are fixed wide in fear, شَاخِصَةٌ أَبْصَارُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا, an opposite posture.
The section says today's eyes can still look before the Day when they are humbled; this verse reverses that present ability by saying the one who turns from remembrance will be raised blind.
The section's gaze can turn freely across the world; here the Prophet's sight neither swerved nor exceeded, مَا زَاغَ الْبَصَرُ وَمَا طَغَى, a stated limit on a particular vision.

The section names the Lord-directed gaze of 75:23; here Moses asks to see God and is told he will not see Him, while the mountain crumbles at the manifestation. It marks a boundary around the image of looking toward God.
The source section cites a gaze directed toward the Lord; this ayah sets a boundary by saying eyes do not encompass Him, clarifying that directed sight is not exhaustive grasp.
The section sets humbled faces against the surah's promised ease; this verse calls the hidden reward قُرَّةَ أَعْيُنٍ, a specific afterlife reversal from eyes lowered in disgrace to delight.

The section joins the root خ ش ع to humbled eyes and separately looks at mountains; this verse says a mountain would be seen خَاشِعًا and split from awe of the Qur'an, bringing those two image details together.
The source section names خ ش ع for a visible humbled gaze; here the heart is asked to become humble at God's remembrance, shifting the same root from the eye's outward posture to inward reception.

This verse says those who hear the Qur'an fall in prostration and grow in خشوع; it offers a deliberate, devotional lowering that parallels the section's downward eye posture while differing from shame.
The verse names livestock as created for warmth, other benefits, and food; it gives a concrete human relation to the animal creation the section asks readers to inspect.
The verse describes livestock carrying loads to distant places, a specific use of large animals that adds transport to the camel's created form in the section.
The verse names horses, mules, and donkeys for riding and adornment and says God creates what people do not know; it broadens the section's view of animals made for human use.
This verse calls livestock a lesson and describes drink from their bellies and other benefits; it offers a concrete animal scene beside the camel selected for observation.
This verse names sacrificial camels as signs from God and tells people to mention His name over them; it adds a ritual use to the camel the section makes an object of attention.
This verse says God created pairs and made ships and livestock mounts for people; it gives an explicit use for the animal creation the section asks readers to consider.
This verse specifies settling on the backs of mounts and remembering God's favor, a concrete camel-adjacent use that follows the section's question about the animal.
The source section's root ع ي ن names both eye and spring; this verse says eyes overflow with tears, making the eye itself a source of flowing water beside the spring-as-eye image.
The source section's eye/spring root meets an eye that pours tears, تَفِيضُ مِنَ الدَّمْعِ أَعْيُنُهُمْ; here flowing water comes from eyes in response to the message.
After this verse's trembling hearts, 79:9 says the eyes are humbled; the cited ayah adds the inner dread surrounding the downcast gaze.
This verse calls them to prostrate and says they cannot; the following 68:43 contributes the humbled eyes, linking failed bodily submission to the gaze's humiliation.
This verse has people rushing toward the caller; 70:44 then supplies the humbled eyes and disgrace, continuing the resurrection scene of the section.
After 14:42 says eyes stare, this verse adds heads lifted and eyelids not returning; it sharpens the fixed, terrified gaze that contrasts with the section's lowered one.
The section's question asks people to read signs by looking; this verse says some see every sign yet will not believe, showing how an open gaze can remain unresponsive.
The section's root ع ي ن names the eye and its gaze; here eyes are covered from God's reminder, a concrete case where physical eyes fail to receive what is shown.
The section's thoughtful looking joins eye and insight; this verse says blindness is in hearts, not the eyes, distinguishing bodily sight from the perception its question demands.
The source section's couch-side looking recurs here for the righteous; set beside the section's fire-facing hidden glance, the same verb marks opposite destinies.
The source section develops the eye as the organ of gaze; here Jacob's eyes turn white from grief, a specific loss of sight that contrasts with the gaze still available before the Day.

The source section's free gaze is directed to created signs; this verse sets a boundary on where the eye turns, telling the Prophet not to let his eyes pass beyond the believers toward worldly adornment.
The section presents a gaze available for reflection; this verse warns against extending the eyes toward worldly enjoyments, a specific limit on free looking.
This verse repeats the boundary on extending one's eyes toward worldly adornment; it makes the section's freedom to look a responsibility about what draws the gaze.
The source section's root ع ي ن names an eye and is heard in the spring of 88:12; here the same spring noun places the God-fearing in gardens and springs.
The source section hears eye within the spring noun; this verse shows gardens and springs among what Pharaoh's people leave behind, giving the spring word a worldly, passing scene.
The source section names the eye-and-spring relation; here gardens and springs form part of the material prosperity of the people of ʿAd.
The source section's spring word echoes here in gardens and springs among the crops and palms, a concrete scene of provision from the land.
The source section hears the eye sense in its spring; here gardens and date palms are set in the earth and springs are made to gush from it.
The source section's water-visible-to-eyes gloss for ع ي ن meets a cup of مَعِين here, a drink presented as flowing from a spring in the garden.
The source section's spring-as-eye word appears in the gardens and springs left by Pharaoh's people; the scene makes earthly abundance visibly abandoned and passing.
The source section's spring noun echoes in this promised garden scene, where the God-fearing are placed among gardens and springs.
The section identifies the spring word عَيْن with the eye; here the righteous are placed in gardens and springs, making the same water-source image part of the afterlife reward.
The source section's water-visible-to-eyes gloss for ع ي ن meets a cup of مَعِين, bringing flowing spring water into the garden's drinking scene.
This verse names a garden spring عَيْنًا and calls it Salsabil; it repeats the source section's spring-as-eye word in a paradise scene.
The source section's spring noun echoes in the righteous dwelling among shade and springs, pairing its water image with shelter.
The source section's عين means both eye and spring; here the close ones drink from a spring, عَيْنًا, placing that double sense in a garden of reward.
Continuing the sky-and-earth signs of 50:6 and 50:7, this verse calls them insight and reminder; it names the kind of reflective seeing the source section asks of its reader.
This verse completes the rain-and-growth scene begun in 50:9 by naming provision and revival of dead land as a sign of emergence, joining the section's creation-gaze to resurrection.
This verse completes the sky's ordering with its dark night and brought-out daylight, extending the upward scene from 79:28.
This verse adds water and pasture from the spread earth of 79:30, giving visible life to the ground the section asks readers to inspect.
This verse completes the provision scene by naming livelihood for people and their livestock; it links the preceding pasture and the section's camel to sustenance.
This verse gives the source of human creation as a flowing fluid, answering the inspection command in 86:5 with a concrete created substance.
Continuing the creation answer of 86:5 and 86:6, this verse identifies where that fluid emerges, making the human body itself an object of careful looking.
Following the command to look at food in 80:24, this verse shows rain poured down, the first step in the provisioning scene.
The food sequence from 80:24 continues as the earth is split open, supplying the ground-level scene behind the section's look toward earth.
This verse continues the inspected food scene with grain, a visible product of the earth.
The next verse adds grapes and edible greens to the food grown from the earth.
This verse adds olive and date palms to the same sequence of visible crops.
The food passage continues with densely planted gardens, extending the visible growth scene.
This verse adds fruit and pasture, connecting the earth's growth to the camel and livestock in the section.
This verse completes the sequence by naming provision for people and their livestock; it connects the observed crops to the section's created camel.
The signs listed here include the heavens and earth, night and day, rain, revived ground, and animals; their observable combination parallels the section's four-direction survey.
This verse calls the creation of heavens and earth and the alternation of night and day signs for reflection, stating the contemplative response invited by the section's look.
This verse says the reflective people think about the creation of the heavens and earth, continuing 3:190's invitation to read visible creation.
The verse describes the earth spread out with mountains, rivers, and paired fruits, then calls these signs for people who reflect, matching the section's earth-and-mountain view.
This verse lists crops, olives, palms, grapes, and fruits as signs for people who think; it supplies a specific plant field for the section's gaze at creation and provision.
This verse adds night, day, sun, moon, and stars as signs, expanding the sky-side objects of the section's free gaze.
This verse adds the varied things made on earth as signs for people who remember, continuing the section's invitation to inspect the ground.
This verse says mountains were set in the earth and paths made through them, then describes the sky as a protected roof; it combines the section's upward and downward field.
The source section defines the sky by what is above and shades; this verse calls it a protected ceiling, while people turn away from its signs, a specific boundary on the gaze.
This verse calls earth a resting place and mentions paths through it for guidance, a concrete counterpart to looking down at the shaped ground.
The verse says the sky was raised, وَالسَّمَاءَ رَفَعَهَا, matching exactly the upward direction and lifting described in the source section.
This verse says the earth was laid out for living creatures, an explicit counterpart to the section's view of earth spread below.
The verse says the sky was built and expanded, directly extending the section's upward look at how the sky was raised.
This verse says the earth was spread out; its wording gives another direct formulation of the ground-side scene in the source section.
The verse asks how God created seven skies layered above, repeating the source section's question about the construction of the sky.
Continuing the sky scene, this verse places the moon as light within it and the sun as a lamp, giving visible particulars above the viewer.
The verse asks whether earth was made a resting place, a direct formulation of the ground made accessible to those looking down.
This verse calls mountains pegs, giving an account of their placement that complements the section's question about how mountains were raised.
This verse says the earth was spread, mountains set, and plants made to grow in measured balance, gathering the earth-side signs the section presents.
This verse says mountains were placed so the earth would not shake, and mentions rivers and routes, tying the section's raised mountains and earthly orientation together.
Following the earth's routes, this verse mentions landmarks and stars used for guidance, joining the section's looked-at sky and ground to orientation.
The source section's gloss for the sky includes what is above and shades people; this verse explicitly describes shade as provision within the created world.
The source section's gloss for the sky mentions what shades; this verse asks the reader to see how God extends the shade and makes the sun a guide.
After 25:45 shows the stretched shade, this verse describes its gradual withdrawal, making the relation between sky-light and ground visible.
This verse pairs the earth as a resting place with the sky as a canopy and rain yielding fruit, matching the section's contrast between ground below and sky above.
The verse asks who made heavens and earth and sent rain to grow a beautiful garden; it gives a specific created landscape for the section's reflective gaze.
This verse names lightning and rain from the sky and the revival of earth as signs, a concrete upward-and-downward scene for attentive sight.
This verse says heavens and earth stand by God's command and that people will emerge from earth, linking the observed cosmos to resurrection.
This verse describes winds and rain bringing dead land back to life, a visible earth-and-revival scene that supports the section's link between looking and return.
The verse follows water from the sky into earth and shows varied crops growing and drying; it makes the changing ground a visible sign beside the section's spring and earth.
This verse says God's signs will be shown in horizons and within people until truth becomes clear, a concise statement of the outward and inward seeing the section stages.
The verse says there are signs in heavens and earth, naming the same broad visible field the section directs the gaze across.
The verse locates signs in human creation and animals spread through the earth, connecting its camel example to the wider created animal world.
This verse adds night and day, rain, revived earth, and winds as signs, matching specific sky-and-earth phenomena in the section's panorama.

The section contrasts eyes cast down on the Last Day with a gaze free to inspect creation; this verse contrasts one walking face-down with one walking upright, turning bodily direction into a figure for guidance.
This verse says God formed people and gave them hearing, sight, and hearts, but few are grateful; it ties the eye that can look to the responsibility to perceive.
This verse continues the earth's growth scene from 50:9 with tall date palms and layered fruit, a specific visible feature of provision.
This verse describes radiant faces immediately before 75:23 says they look toward their Lord; it supplies the face's joyful state around the gaze named by the section.
After 79:9 shows humbled eyes on the Day, this verse records the deniers asking whether they will be returned after becoming decayed bones, grounding the gaze in dispute over resurrection.
This verse says faces are humbled before the Ever-Living, linking the section's lowered gaze to a broader posture of submission on the Day; its own contribution is the face's abasement before God.
The section's source gloss connects looking with sight and insight; this verse contrasts whoever sees with whoever is blind, making explicit the boundary between perception and mere looking.
This verse asks whether people see that God created livestock for them; it gives a direct animal-creation counterpart to the camel the section invites them to inspect.
This verse asks readers to see birds held in the sky, adding a specific creature-in-the-sky scene beside the section's camel and raised-sky view.
This verse makes stars signs for finding one's way through land and sea at night, connecting the section's upward look at the sky with orientation on the earth below.
This verse asks whether people see that God begins creation and repeats it; the next 29:20 adds travel across the earth to inspect how creation began, tying visible creation to return.
This verse joins life emerging from death to earth revived after death and says people will be brought forth likewise, a specific earth-and-resurrection parallel to the section's gaze.
Before 30:50 tells people to look at God's mercy in reviving earth, this verse contributes the winds, clouds, and rain that make the land revive.
After 30:50's revived earth, this verse adds the contrary sight of vegetation yellowing after a wind; it also says the viewers remain ungrateful.
This verse calls the revived dead land and its grain a sign; the next 36:34 adds gardens and springs, so this ayah contributes the earth-revival scene beside the section's spring image.
Before 40:19 names God's knowledge of furtive eyes, this verse contributes the approaching Day, with hearts at throats and people in dread, grounding the hidden glance in judgment.
The section's eye image includes humbled sight and paradise; this verse says eyes delight in the garden's provision, a specific afterlife reversal from the downcast gaze.

The source section's root خ ش ع is glossed through a gaze lowered to earth; this verse uses that root for humility in prayer, a devotional counterpart to the humbled gaze, though it does not itself mention the eyes.
